questions.q: What are the three parts of a typical test?
options: Arrange a small input, act by calling the function, assert the result
questions.explain: A test sets up a small input, calls the code under test, and asserts that the output matches what you expect.

questions.q: A refactor changes revenue from quantity * unit_price to quantity + unit_price. What happens to a test asserting revenue == [10.0, 12.0] for quantities [2, 3] and prices [5.0, 4.0]?
options: It still passes because the columns exist
It fails, because the new result is [7.0, 7.0]
questions.explain: 2 + 5 = 7 and 3 + 4 = 7, so the assertion no longer matches [10.0, 12.0] and the test fails, exposing the bug.

questions.explain: assert_frame_equal is built for testing: it raises an AssertionError describing the difference when two DataFrames don't match.

questions.q: What is the difference between testing your code and checking your data?
options: Tests use small made-up inputs to verify functions; data checks assert properties of the real incoming data
They are exactly the same thing
Tests only work on CSV files; data checks only work on databases
Data checks are only run by pytest
questions.explain: Tests verify that your logic is correct on inputs you control. Data checks, like unique IDs or non-negative revenue, verify the actual data each time it arrives.

questions.q: With limited time, which should you test first?
options: Business rules, edge cases such as missing values and duplicates, and bugs you have already fixed
questions.explain: Focus on logic where a mistake costs the most, on inputs that commonly break code, and on regressions of past bugs.
